extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a claimed invention satisfies the utility requirement under 35 U.S.C. 101 (and related 35 U.S.C. 112 enablement/best-mode issues), including when examiner rejections for lack of utility are appropriate and what evidence/analysis is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claim utility inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim is treated as claiming an invention that has utility if the independent claim from which the dependent claim depends is drawn to the same statutory class of invention as the dependent claim and the independent claim defines an invention having utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: where the utility specified for the invention defined in a dependent claim differs from that indicated for the invention defined in the independent claim. If dependent/species utility differs, examiner must consider separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic claim when species utility established
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an applicant has established utility for a species that falls within an identified genus of compounds, a generic claim covering the genus should generally be treated as sufficient under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only impose rejection on generic claim if it can be established that other species clearly encompassed by the claim do not have utility; encourage applicant to amend generic claim to exclude species that lack utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: One credible assertion suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant need only make one credible assertion of specific utility for the claimed invention to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112; additional statements of utility, even if not 'credible', do not render the claimed invention lacking in utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite case law (e.g., Raytheon v. Roper, In re Gottlieb). If at least one stated objective is met, utility under 35 U.S.C. 101 is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant statements alone not basis for rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made by the applicant in the specification or incident to prosecution cannot, standing alone, be the basis for a lack of utility rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 or 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office should not require applicants to strike nonessential statements relating to utility; examiners should be careful not to read unclaimed results, limitations, or embodiments into claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify asserted or well-established utility on initial exam
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon initial examination, the examiner should review the specification to determine if there are any statements asserting that the claimed invention is useful for any particular purpose and whether disclosure identifies a specific and substantial utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete disclosure should include a statement identifying a specific and substantial utility; examiner should locate and evaluate any such statements in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific and substantial utility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of utility must be 'specific and substantial': it should fully and clearly explain why the applicant asserts the invention is useful and enable one ordinarily skilled in the art to understand why the applicant asserts the claimed invention is useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic assertions (e.g., 'biological activity', 'pharmacological effects') without explaining why that activity is useful are insufficient (citing Brenner v. Manson, In re Ziegler, In re Kirk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to identify specific and substantial utility -> rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Except where an invention has a well-established utility, failure to specifically identify why an invention is believed useful renders the claimed invention deficient under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided where general statements were insufficient; examiner should issue appropriate rejections and tie to enablement/best-mode concerns where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-established utility definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention has a well-established utility if (i) a person of ordinary skill in the art would immediately appreciate why the invention is useful based on the characteristics of the invention, and (ii) the utility is specific, substantial, and credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If well-established, rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and related 112 grounds based on lack of an asserted specific and substantial utility should not be imposed (example: cloning insulin).

rubrics_metrics.name: When examiner should reject for lack of recognized utility
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person of ordinary skill would not immediately recognize a specific and substantial utility for the claimed invention based on its characteristics or applicant statements, the examiner should reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejection should clearly indicate the basis (failure to identify specific and substantial utility) and specify that applicant must reply indicating why invention is believed useful and where support is in the specification as filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of utility from applicant assertion (Langer test)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant's assertion of utility creates a presumption of utility sufficient to satisfy the utility requirement unless there is reason for one skilled in the art to question the objective truth of the statement of utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not begin by questioning truth; start by asking whether there is any reason to question the truth. Apply Langer/Marzocchi formulations and related case law (In re Langer, In re Marzocchi, In re Brana).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard to overcome presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: To overcome the presumption of utility, Office personnel must show by a preponderance of the totality of the evidence that it is more likely than not that one of ordinary skill in the art would question the truth of the applicant's asserted utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office must present factual evidence and reasoning sufficient to show the statement would be considered false by a person of ordinary skill; applicant's supporting facts and reasoning must be countered by Office evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility of asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: An asserted utility is credible (believable to a person of ordinary skill) unless (A) the logic underlying the assertion is seriously flawed, or (B) the facts upon which the assertion is based are inconsistent with the logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credibility depends on reliability of logic and facts offered by applicant; 'incredible utility' is a conclusion after evaluating assertion and evidence—not a starting presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incredible utility circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions will be found not credible where they are incredible in view of contemporary knowledge (e.g., assertion could only be true if it violated scientific principles or laws of nature) or where facts contradict the claimed utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special care with therapeutic utilities: prior lack of success or absence of an animal model alone should not be sole basis for challenging asserted utility. Courts have sustained rejections when assertions defy scientific principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial burden and prima facie requirement on the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: To properly reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 the Office must (A) make a prima facie showing that the claimed invention lacks utility, and (B) provide sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon in establishing that prima facie showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prima facie showing must be set forth in a well-reasoned statement; provide documentary evidence where possible (journals, treatises, patents) or explain scientific basis for factual conclusions when documentary evidence unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie elements for lack of specific/substantial utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the asserted utility is not specific or substantial, the prima facie showing must establish that it is more likely than not a person of ordinary skill would not consider any asserted utility to be specific and substantial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prima facie showing must include: (A) explanation of reasoning; (B) support for factual findings; (C) evaluation of all relevant evidence of record, including utilities in the closest prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie elements for lack of credible utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the asserted specific and substantial utility is not credible, prima facie showing must establish it is more likely than not that a person skilled in the art would not consider credible any asserted specific and substantial utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prima facie showing must include: (A) explanation of reasoning; (B) support for factual findings; (C) evaluation of all relevant evidence of record, including closest prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing when no asserted or well-established utility
rubrics_metrics.description: When no specific and substantial utility is disclosed or well-established, a prima facie showing need only establish that applicant has not asserted a utility and that, on the record, there is no known well-established utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specificity in rejection so applicant can identify and address the Office's assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity in setting forth rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must use specificity in initial rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and support any factual conclusions made in the prima facie showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specificity permits applicant to identify assumptions and address them properly; use the provided form paragraphs and formats (7.05.02 - 7.05.04 and Formats A/B/C) with the bracketed insert guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph guidance for utility rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Use form paragraphs 7.05.02 (Utility Lacking), 7.05.03 (Inoperative), and 7.05.04 (Utility Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112) to reject claims for failure to satisfy utility requirement, with bracketed inserts specifying explanations and wording (e.g., 'specific and substantial', 'credible').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Format A/B/C instructions: which inserts to use, how to handle multiple utilities, and examiner notes regarding enablement overlap and use of Wands factors for enablement rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: When examiner may request evidentiary support from applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: In appropriate situations, the Office may require an applicant to substantiate an asserted utility (e.g., when operativeness would be deemed unlikely by one of ordinary skill), but such requests should be imposed rarely and only if necessary to support scientific credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When requesting evidence, indicate why factual record is defective relative to applicant assertions and suggest what type of evidentiary showing can remedy the problem; courts permit higher burden where asserted utility appears incredible or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on examiner demands for test data
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper for the examiner to demand further test data when the PTO's own evidence would make such data redundant or when the demand would unduly burden the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only after the PTO provides evidence showing one of ordinary skill would reasonably doubt the asserted utility does the burden shift to applicant to provide rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant rebuttal options and evidence standards
rubrics_metrics.description: After a proper prima facie showing, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut via claim amendments, arguments, new evidence in affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132, or printed publications. New evidence must be relevant to issues raised in the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations that merely state conclusions without establishing nexus to supporting evidence or that are mere opinions may have limited probative value (citing In re Grunwell, In re Buchner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner evaluation of applicant reply
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must review the original disclosure, evidence relied upon for the prima facie showing, claim amendments, and any new reasoning/evidence provided; recognize, fully consider and respond to each substantive element of any response to a rejection based on lack of utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If totality of record would make asserted utility credible to a person of ordinary skill, the Office cannot maintain the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable correlation suffices for evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no predetermined amount/character of evidence required to support an asserted utility; evidence is sufficient if, considered as a whole, it leads a person of ordinary skill to conclude the asserted utility is more likely than not true — i.e., a reasonable correlation between evidence and asserted utility is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant need not prove utility beyond reasonable doubt or by statistical certainty; evidence can include statistically relevant data, reasoning, publications, or combinations thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special considerations for therapeutic/pharmacological utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: For therapeutic or pharmacological utilities, evidence of pharmacological/biological activity is relevant if there is a reasonable correlation between the activity and the asserted therapeutic utility; courts have reversed rejections where applicants provided reasonable supporting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may rely on animal testing, in vitro data, structural similarity to known therapeutics, statistical data, published articles, reasoning, or combinations to establish reasonable correlation; not required to provide human clinical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural similarity as supportive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of close structural similarity to compounds known to have a particular therapeutic utility can support an assertion of therapeutic utility for a new compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both the existence of the structural relationship and the reasoning explaining why the structural similarity is relevant to the asserted utility (citing In re Jolles and related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: In vitro and animal testing generally sufficient for therapeutic utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Data from in vitro or animal testing is generally sufficient to support an asserted therapeutic utility, provided there is a reasonable evidentiary correlation to the claimed human therapeutic use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such data should be considered along with other evidence and reasoning; courts recognize animal/in vitro data as relevant for predicting human therapeutic response when a reasonable correlation exists.
